headline: High risk: shared filesystem and broad code-execution defaults make prompt injection, leakage, and destructive cross-agent actions plausible.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write files, and B explicitly shares state via filesystem while A has a workspace and MCP surfaces. That creates a default content-bridging path where attacker-controlled files from A can be treated as instructions by B. A’s sandboxing helps, but B has no comparable isolation by default.
conditions: IF A writes instruction-like content into the shared filesystem
IF B ingests file contents as trusted prompts or commands
IF the pair is run without an external provenance filter
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Disable automatic file-to-prompt ingestion
Add provenance tags to shared files
Run B in a read-only mount for A’s outputs
requires-engineering: enforce content sanitization at the orchestrator

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches API keys, private keys, bearer tokens, and conversation history, while B can read the entire user filesystem and has broad network egress. In default configurations, A’s workspace and secrets can be exposed to B and then transmitted onward. A’s strict sandboxing does not prevent leakage through the shared local filesystem.
conditions: IF A stores secrets or conversation history in its workspace
IF B is granted access to the same filesystem tree
IF B forwards file contents to a configured model provider or remote service
mitigations: Move secrets out of shared paths
Mount A’s workspace read-only for B
Redact sensitive files before B runs
Restrict B network egress for shared directories
requires-engineering: add per-file access controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, and git-state modification. B’s shared state is via filesystem, and A supports multiple instances with durable memory namespaces, so concurrent writes can collide and corrupt work or git history. No locking mechanism is documented in either profile.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or directory
IF either agent modifies git state without external locking
mitigations: Use separate clones per agent
Serialize git operations with a lock file
Assign disjoint output directories
Pause one agent during writes
requires-engineering: add transactional workspace coordination

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can generate web, webhook, and workspace-derived outputs, and B can act on local files and shell commands. If B treats A’s outputs as authoritative, A’s mistakes can cascade into destructive local actions or commits. B’s confirmation-per-code-block helps, but --auto_run can remove that safeguard and A’s outputs remain unverified.
conditions: IF B consumes A-generated text as instructions or facts
IF B is run with auto-run or equivalent confirmation bypass
IF A produces incorrect commands, paths, or claims
mitigations: Require human review before execution
Disable auto-run on B
Insert a verification step between agents
Limit A to advisory output only
requires-engineering: add schema validation for handoff messages

E_compliance.rationale: A handles audit logs, conversation history, memory, and secrets; B can access anything on the local machine and uses model providers configured by the user. That creates a plausible retention and residency mismatch if regulated data from A is exposed to B and then sent to third-party providers. No specific certifications or DPA controls are documented here, so uncertainty pushes upward.
conditions: IF regulated data is present in A’s workspace or logs
IF B sends that data to a remote model provider
IF retention or deletion policies differ between the two agents
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared folders
Use a local-only model for B
Shorten log retention on both agents
Document a common deletion workflow
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls
